reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and standard clinical immunology texts
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of lysosomal trafficking caused by biallelic variants in LYST, disrupting the size and function of lysosome-related organelles
The pathognomonic finding is giant intracytoplasmic granules in neutrophils and other leucocytes on a peripheral blood film
Partial oculocutaneous albinism with silvery hair and photophobia results from abnormal melanosome distribution
Recurrent pyogenic infections, especially of skin and respiratory tract, reflect defective neutrophil chemotaxis and impaired natural killer and cytotoxic T-cell function
A bleeding tendency arises from a platelet storage-pool defect
Most patients enter an accelerated phase resembling haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, with fever, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphohistiocytic infiltration
A minority present later with a milder course dominated by progressive neurological deterioration
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation can correct the immune and haematological features but does not prevent the neurological decline
reference.pathophysiology: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in LYST, which encodes a regulator of lysosomal and lysosome-related organelle trafficking. Defective vesicle fission and fusion produce the characteristic giant granules, impair melanosome transfer (albinism), degranulation of cytotoxic lymphocytes and natural killer cells (immunodeficiency and predisposition to the accelerated phase), platelet dense-granule function (bleeding), and neuronal membrane trafficking (neurodegeneration).
additionalInvestigations: Peripheral blood film for giant granules in leucocytes
Examination of a hair shaft for characteristic pigment clumping
Natural killer cell and cytotoxic lymphocyte function assays
Full blood count, ferritin, triglycerides and fibrinogen to detect the accelerated (haemophagocytic) phase
Platelet function testing and bleeding assessment
redFlags: Fever with cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly and rising ferritin suggesting the accelerated phase
Overwhelming or recurrent severe pyogenic infection
Uncontrolled bleeding from the platelet storage-pool defect
reference.prognosis: Without haematopoietic stem cell transplantation most children die in the first decade, usually during the accelerated phase or from infection. Transplantation restores immune and haematological function and prevents the accelerated phase but does not halt the later progressive neurological disease.
pitfalls: Missing the giant leucocyte granules on the blood film
Attributing the albinism to a non-syndromic cause and overlooking the immunodeficiency
Failing to recognise and promptly treat the accelerated (haemophagocytic) phase
Assuming transplantation will prevent the neurological decline
management: Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the definitive treatment, best performed before the accelerated phase, to correct the immunodeficiency and cytopenias
Manage the accelerated haemophagocytic phase with HLH-directed immunochemotherapy such as corticosteroids, etoposide and ciclosporin as a bridge to transplantation
Prevent and promptly treat recurrent pyogenic skin and respiratory infections with antimicrobials and prophylaxis where indicated
Bleeding precautions for the platelet storage-pool defect, avoiding antiplatelet drugs and using platelet transfusion or desmopressin to cover procedures
Photoprotection for partial oculocutaneous albinism with sun avoidance, sunscreen and tinted lenses
Surveillance for the accelerated phase with blood counts, ferritin, triglycerides and fibrinogen, and long-term neurological monitoring since transplantation does not prevent later neurodegeneration
Multidisciplinary immunology, haematology and clinical genetics input
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with carrier testing of relatives
